describing-distributions-s1.title: Commute times of 60 workers

plot.label: Histogram of the one-way commute times of 60 workers in bins 5 minutes wide, from 0 to 70 minutes: most between 5 and 25 minutes, a long tail to the right, and one value between 65 and 70 minutes

describing-distributions-s1.text: A histogram of the one-way commute times of 60 workers at a hospital, in bins 5 minutes wide (invented data).

describing-distributions-s2.title: Heights of 30 athletes

plot.label: Histogram of the heights of 30 athletes in bins 5 centimeters wide: one group from 145 to 165 centimeters, an empty stretch from 165 to 180, and a second group from 180 to 205 centimeters

describing-distributions-s2.text: A sports camp measured the heights of the 30 athletes in two of its groups, in centimeters (invented data).

items.q: What is the shape of the distribution of commute times?

why.correct: The tail stretches toward the larger values, so the distribution is skewed right (toward the tail).
options: Skew is named for the tail, not the peak. The long tail here points right.
Right: most times are short, and the bars trail off in a long tail toward the longer times on the right.
There is one peak, but the right side stretches much farther than the left, so the shape is not symmetric.
A uniform shape has bars of about equal height; these rise and then fall away.
Skewed left, because the tallest bars are on the left side
Skewed right
Roughly symmetric, with one peak between 10 and 15 minutes
Uniform, since each bin holds a few of the workers

items.q: Which unusual feature does the histogram show?

why.correct: The empty bins from 45 to 65 minutes form a gap, and the lone commute between 65 and 70 is a possible outlier.
options: The bars fall steadily from 10 to 45 minutes; there is no second peak.
The bar from 0 to 5 joins the rest of the data; it does not stand apart.
The empty bins from 45 to 65 and the lone bar after them stand out.
Right: one worker’s commute sits far from the rest, so it is a possible outlier.
A second peak between 30 and 35 minutes, making it bimodal
A cluster of commutes below 5 minutes that stands apart
No unusual features, as the bars decrease steadily
A gap from 45 to 65 minutes, then one commute between 65 and 70

items.q: About where is the center of the distribution, the value with half the commutes below it?

why.correct: Count from the left: $3 + 10 + 14 = 27$ commutes under 15 minutes and $27 + 11 = 38$ under 20. The middle (the 30th and 31st values) is in the 15 to 20 bin.
options: Right: 27 commutes are under 15 minutes and 38 are under 20, so the 30th and 31st values fall in the 15 to 20 bin.
The tallest bar is the most common bin, not the middle of the data.
Halfway along the axis is not the middle of the data; the commutes bunch at the low end.
By 20 minutes, 38 of the 60 commutes have already been counted, more than half.
Between 15 and 20 minutes
Between 10 and 15 minutes, the tallest bar
About 35 minutes, halfway between 0 and 70
Between 20 and 25 minutes, past the peak

items.q: Which description of the distribution is the most complete?

why.correct: A full description covers shape, center, spread and unusual features, each with numbers, and names the variable in context.
options: It has numbers but no context: it never says these are commute times in minutes.
It gives shape and context but no center, spread or unusual features, and it adds a claim the data do not show.
Right: it gives shape, center, spread and unusual features, all in context with numbers.
It reads bars instead of describing shape, center and spread.
The distribution is skewed right with a center between 15 and 20 and an outlier between 65 and 70; most of the values are from 5 to 30, so the spread is large
The commute times of the 60 workers are skewed to the right, which tells us that most of the hospital’s workers live a short drive from work
The distribution of commute times is skewed right with a center between 15 and 20 minutes; most commutes take 5 to 30 minutes, with a gap and one possible outlier between 65 and 70 minutes
The histogram of commute times has a tallest bar from 10 to 15 minutes and a shortest bar from 40 to 45 minutes, with many bars between them

items.q: What is the shape of the distribution of heights?

why.correct: Two peaks with a gap between them make the distribution bimodal.
options: A long tail would be a few large values trailing off; here there is a whole second group.
A uniform shape has bars of about equal height everywhere; this histogram has an empty stretch in the middle.
Right: there are two separate peaks, one near 155 cm and one near 190 cm.
The two sides match, but there are two peaks and almost no one near 175.
Skewed right, because the heights go up to 202 centimeters
Uniform, since both groups have about the same number of athletes
Bimodal
Roughly symmetric and unimodal, centered near 175 centimeters

items.q: What is the most likely explanation for the shape of this distribution?

why.correct: Two clusters usually point to two kinds of individuals in one data set. Here that is two sports.
options: Right: a bimodal distribution often signals that two groups have been mixed together, such as gymnasts and basketball players.
Heights in inches would be near 60 to 80, far below the values here.
Rounding would change bars a little; it would not create two groups 30 cm apart.
That would push the data up, not split it into two separate groups.
The athletes come from two sports with very different typical heights
Some athletes were measured in inches instead of centimeters
The heights were rounded to the nearest 5 centimeters
Tall athletes are more likely to be chosen for the camp

items.q: Which unusual feature does the histogram show?

why.correct: The empty bins between about 165 and 180 cm are a gap between two clusters.
options: 202 is close to the other tall athletes, inside the upper cluster.
148 sits with the lower cluster of heights.
The stretch from 165 to 180 is empty, so the heights are far from uniform.
Right: the empty bins between the two clusters form a gap.
An outlier at 202 centimeters, the tallest athlete in the camp
An outlier at 148 centimeters, the shortest athlete in the camp
A uniform stretch of heights between 150 and 200 centimeters
A gap: no athlete is between 165 and 180 centimeters

items.q: A coach says, "A typical athlete at this camp is about 175 cm tall." Why is this a poor summary?

why.correct: In a bimodal distribution a single center can fall in a gap where there are no values. Describe each cluster separately.
options: The problem is not the size of 175 but that no athlete is near it.
Right: a single center hides the two groups. It is better to describe each group on its own.
Centers can be given in any unit; this one just falls in the gap.
The unit does not matter; a center in the gap misleads in any unit.
175 centimeters is too tall to be a typical height for an athlete
Hardly anyone is near 175; the heights form two groups
A center is not defined for heights measured in centimeters
The coach should have used inches to describe the athletes

items.q: Scores on an easy quiz: most students score 9 or 10 out of 10, and a few score much lower. What shape is the distribution?

why.correct: A tail toward the low values makes the distribution skewed left. Name the skew for the tail, not for where most values are.
options: Right: the few low scores form a tail toward the smaller values, on the left.
Skew is named for the tail. The tail points to the low scores, so the skew is left.
Scores cannot go above 10, so the low tail has no match on the right.
Possible values are not the same as how often they occur; most scores pile up at 9 and 10.
Skewed left
Skewed right, because most of the scores are high ones
Roughly symmetric around a score of 9 out of 10
Uniform, since each score from 0 to 10 is possible

items.q: A distribution is skewed right. What does that tell you?

why.correct: Skewed right tells you the tail is on the right, toward the larger values.
options: In a right-skewed distribution most values are on the left; the tail is on the right.
Two peaks describe a bimodal shape, not skew.
Right: "skewed right" names the direction of the tail.
A long tail is not the same as outliers, and outliers are not simply removed.
Most of the values are on the right side of the graph
The graph has two separate peaks with a gap
A long tail stretches toward the larger values
The largest values are outliers to be removed

items.q: A spinner lands on the numbers 1 to 8 with no number favored. After 800 spins, which shape do you expect for a histogram of the results?

why.correct: When each value occurs about equally often, the bars are about level: a uniform shape.
options: No number is favored, so there is no reason for a tail.
Right: each number should come up about 100 times, so the bars are about the same height.
The ends of the spinner are not favored, so there is no reason for two peaks.
A peak in the middle would show middle numbers coming up more often, but each number is equally favored.
Skewed right, toward the larger numbers
Roughly uniform
Bimodal, with peaks at 1 and at 8
Mound-shaped with a peak near 4 or 5

items.q: The ages of members of club A run from 40 to 60 years. The ages in club B run from 10 to 90 years. Which statement compares their spread?

why.correct: Spread (variability) describes how far apart the values are: from 10 to 90 is far wider than from 40 to 60.
options: Spread is about how far apart values are, not how large they are.
Club B includes children and much older adults, so its ages are more spread out.
The range of values is enough here to see that B is more spread out.
Right: B’s ages cover 80 years and A’s cover 20.
Club A’s ages vary more, since its members are older
The spreads are the same, since both clubs contain adults
Spread is impossible to compare without the shape of each club
Club B’s ages vary more than club A’s ages do

why.correct: An outlier is a value that falls far outside the overall pattern. Investigate it; do not simply delete it.
options: The largest value is an outlier only if it is far from the others.
Right: an outlier stands apart from the rest of the distribution.
An outlier may be a real value; investigate it rather than deleting it.
The most common value is the peak (mode), the opposite of an outlier.
The largest value in any data set, whatever its distance from the rest
A value that falls far from the overall pattern of the data
A value that was recorded by mistake and is removed
The most common value in the data, where the peak is

items.q: A complete description of a quantitative distribution includes which of these? Select all that apply.

why.correct: Describe shape, center, spread and unusual features, with numbers and in context.
options: Right: for example skewed right, roughly symmetric or bimodal.
Right: a typical value.
Right: how far the values reach or vary.
Names identify individuals; they do not describe a distribution.
Order of collection is not part of describing a distribution.
Colors are a drawing choice, not a feature of the data.
Its shape
Its center, with a number
Its spread, with numbers
The name of each individual in the data set
The order in which the data were collected
The color of each bar in the histogram

items.q: A dotplot of 40 apple weights shows one group from 140 to 170 grams and a second, smaller group from 205 to 220 grams. Which words describe the second group?

why.correct: A bunch of values separated from the rest by empty space is a cluster, and the empty space is a gap.
options: A tail trails off gradually; this group stands on its own after an empty stretch.
The center describes a typical value of the whole data set, not a separate group.
Uniform describes level bars; this is a separate bunch of values.
Right: values bunched together with empty space around them form a cluster; the empty space is a gap.
A long tail of the distribution to the right
A center of the distribution of weights
A uniform part of the distribution
A cluster, set apart by a gap

items.q: A student writes, "The distribution is roughly symmetric, centered at 72, with values from 60 to 85." What is missing for full credit?

why.correct: Shape, center and spread are there, but without context the description could be about anything. Name the variable and units.
options: Right: the description never says what the numbers are, such as heart rates in beats per minute.
A description summarizes; listing every value is not needed.
The student described the shape as roughly symmetric, which can be correct.
One center is enough for a unimodal distribution.
Context: what was measured, and its units
The value of each observation in the data
A statement that the data are skewed
A second center, since a description needs two
